01.note: Rav Nahman cites a teaching that the Ark of the Covenant was hidden in the Temple's Chamber of the Woodshed. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak backs it with a mishna: a priest at work there noticed one floor tile that looked different from the rest. He went to tell his friend, but his soul departed before he could finish, and so they knew for certain the Ark was buried there. Rabbi Helbo says the priest had been banging the floor with his axe; the school of Rabbi Yishmael says two blemished priests were sorting wood when one dropped his axe into that spot, and fire burst out and consumed him.
01.why: The Gemara has been arguing over whether the Ark was taken away into exile, testing whether the verse's words 'there to this day' mean forever. After Ulla's proof is refuted, this account supports the Rabbis' view that the Ark never left but was hidden in the Temple.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Cites the teaching that the Ark was hidden in the Chamber of the Woodshed.

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak
people.about: Supports that teaching with the mishna about the priest who saw the odd floor tile.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥelbo
people.about: Explains that the priest had been striking the floor with his axe.

terms.meaning: The gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the covenant and stood in the innermost room of the Temple.
A storeroom in the Temple courtyard where wood for the altar fire was kept and checked.
Priests with a physical defect, who could not serve at the altar but did other Temple work such as checking the firewood for worms.
The earliest written collection of rabbinic teachings, on which the Gemara comments.

02.note: Reish Lakish tells what happened when gentiles entered the Temple's Sanctuary: they saw images of the cherubs clinging to one another. They carried them out to the market and mocked: these Jews, whose blessing is a blessing and whose curse is a curse, busy themselves with things like this? At once they debased them, and Reish Lakish applies the verse 'All who honored her debase her, because they have seen her nakedness.'
02.why: The discussion has just said that the Temple walls bore carved cherubs embracing 'like a man clinging to his partner', a sign of God's love for Israel. Reish Lakish's account shows how outsiders mocked those same images.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: The Sage who tells what the gentiles did when they saw the cherubs.

terms.meaning: Winged figures that stood over the Ark and were also carved on the Temple walls.
The inner building of the Temple, where only priests could enter.

03.note: Rabbi Yishmael reports that two High Priests from the days of the First Temple were still alive. One said that when he sprinkled the blood on the inner altar he went around it by hand; the other said he walked around it on foot. Each gave a reason for what he had done. The text does not say which of them was right.
03.why: The Gemara has been explaining a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili over how the High Priest goes around the inner altar on Yom Kippur. This report shows the same disagreement between priests who actually served; their two reasons follow in the discussion.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: The Sage who reports what the two surviving High Priests said.

terms.meaning: The chief priest of the Temple, who performed the special Yom Kippur service.
The small gold altar inside the Temple building, used for incense; on Yom Kippur blood was sprinkled on its corners.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the mishna.

04.note: Students put a string of questions to Rabbi Eliezer about the scapegoat: if it fell ill, could its escort carry it on his shoulder? If the escort fell ill, could someone else take it? If it was pushed off the cliff and did not die, should he go down and kill it? Each time he dodged, with answers like 'That goat can carry me and you.' The Sages say yes to all three. They asked him more: about a certain man's place in the World-to-Come, about saving a ewe or a shepherd from a lion, about a mamzer's inheritance, about plastering one's house. Each time he answered with another question.
04.why: The Gemara has just ruled that the man sending the scapegoat may enter the Temple courtyard even if he is impure; these further scapegoat questions follow. Afterward the Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer dodged them because he never said anything he had not heard from his teacher.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage who answers each of his students' questions with an evasion or another question.

terms.meaning: On Yom Kippur one goat was sent into the wilderness carrying the people's sins, and pushed off a cliff.
The life after this one, in which the righteous are rewarded.
A child of a union the Torah forbids, such as adultery, who may not marry most other Jews.
The duty of a man to marry his brother's widow when the brother died without children.

05.note: The Samaritans asked Alexander the Macedonian for permission to destroy the Temple, and he gave it. When Shimon HaTzaddik, the High Priest, heard, he put on the priestly vestments and set out with the nobles of Israel carrying torches; they marched all night toward Alexander's camp. At dawn Alexander saw Shimon, got down from his chariot and bowed to him, saying this man's image led him to victory in his battles. Hearing that the Samaritans wanted to destroy the house where the Jews prayed for him and his kingdom, Alexander handed the Samaritans over to them. They stabbed them in their heels, dragged them behind horses to Mount Gerizim, plowed it and sowed it with leeks, and made that day a festival.
05.why: The Gemara has quoted a ruling that priestly vestments may not be worn outside the Temple. This story, in which Shimon HaTzaddik wears them on the road, challenges that ruling; the Gemara answers that they were only vestment-like garments, or that a time of danger allowed it.

people.name: Shimon HaTzaddik
people.about: The High Priest, who goes out in the priestly vestments to meet Alexander.

people.name: Alexander the Macedonian
people.about: The king who first allows the Temple's destruction, then bows to Shimon HaTzaddik.

terms.meaning: A people living in the land of Israel, rivals of the Jews, who had their own temple on Mount Gerizim.
The sacred garments the priests wore for the Temple service.
The mountain where the Samaritans had their temple.
A town on the road where the two groups met at sunrise.

06.note: A High Priest came out of the Temple and all the people followed him. When they saw Shemaya and Avtalyon, the heads of the Sanhedrin, they left him and walked after them instead. Later, when Shemaya and Avtalyon came to take leave of him, he said: 'Let the descendants of the gentile nations come in peace', mocking their descent from converts. They answered: Let the descendants of the nations come in peace, who act as Aaron did, and let not a descendant of Aaron come in peace, who does not act as Aaron did.
06.why: The mishna describes the people escorting the High Priest home after Yom Kippur, where he made a feast for his loved ones. This incident shows a time the crowd left the High Priest for the Sages.

people.name: Shemaya
people.about: One of the two heads of the Sanhedrin, descended from converts according to the text.

people.name: Avtalyon
people.about: Shemaya's colleague, also a head of the Sanhedrin and of convert descent.

people.name: High Priest
people.about: An unnamed High Priest who mocks the two Sages when the crowd follows them instead of him.

terms.meaning: The highest court and council of Sages.
Moses' brother, the first High Priest, remembered for loving and pursuing peace; all priests descend from him.

07.note: Rav Yehuda found quail among his wine barrels, and Rav Hisda found quail among the logs in his storeroom. Every day Rava's sharecropper brought him a quail. One day he brought none, and Rava wondered why. He went up to the roof and heard a child reciting: 'When I heard, my innards trembled.' Rava concluded that Rav Hisda had died, since it is on account of the teacher that the student eats.
07.why: The Gemara has been describing the quail the Israelites ate in the desert, how small and how rich it was. It moves on to quail that later Sages found as a gift.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who found quail among his wine barrels.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: A Sage who found quail among his logs; Rava's teacher, whose death Rava understands from the missing quail.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rav Hisda's student, whose sharecropper brought him a quail every day.

terms.meaning: A small game bird; the Torah tells that God sent quail to the Israelites in the desert.
A tenant who works another man's fields in exchange for part of the crop.

08.note: The Exilarch came to give a lecture at Rav Natan's study hall in Hagronya. Rafram and all the Sages came; Ravina did not. The next day Rafram, wanting to clear Ravina in the Exilarch's eyes, asked him why he had stayed away. Ravina said his foot hurt. Rafram said he should have worn shoes; Ravina said it was the back of his foot. Then sandals? There was a pool of water on the way. Then cross it in sandals? Ravina replied: does the Master not hold with Rav Ashi, who said one should not cross water in sandals in the first place?
08.why: The Gemara has been asking whether one may cross water on Shabbat in shoes or sandals, and Rav Ashi has just ruled that one should not set out to do so in sandals. Ravina's excuse turns on exactly that ruling.

people.name: Exilarch
people.about: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who came to give the lecture.

people.name: Rafram
people.about: A Sage who attended, and questions Ravina to clear him before the Exilarch.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The Sage who missed the lecture and explains why.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage whose ruling about crossing water in sandals Ravina cites.

terms.meaning: Latin for 'from the start': doing something in the first place, as opposed to accepting it after the fact.

09.note: Ze'eira bar Hama, who had hosted Rabbi Ami, Rabbi Asi, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and all the Sages of Caesarea, said to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's son Rav Yosef: 'Son of a lion, let me tell you a fine thing your father used to do.' On the day before Yom Kippur he soaked a cloth in water and wrung it until it was almost dry, and the next day wiped his face, hands and feet with it. On the day before the Ninth of Av he soaked the cloth, and the next day passed it over his eyes.
09.why: The Gemara has been listing how Sages cooled themselves on Yom Kippur without breaking the ban on bathing. Right after, Rabba bar Mari gives the reverse version of the custom, and the Gemara notes that wringing a cloth is itself forbidden on Yom Kippur.

people.name: Ze'eira bar Ḥama
people.about: The host of many Sages, who tells Rav Yosef about his father's custom.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, to whom the custom is told.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: The Sage whose custom with the damp cloth is described.

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, a fast day on which eating, drinking and bathing are forbidden.
A fast day mourning the Temple's destruction; the text notes its ban on bathing is a rabbinic rule, not a Torah law.

10.note: Rav Giddel bar Menashe of Birei DeNeresh taught in a public lecture that the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. The next year everyone went out, mixed vinegar with water and drank it on Yom Kippur. Rav Giddel heard and became angry. He said: I said one is not liable only after the fact; did I say it may be drunk in the first place? I spoke of a little; did I say a lot? I spoke of pure vinegar; did I say anything about diluted?
10.why: The mishna implies that drinking vinegar on Yom Kippur makes one liable, following Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who says vinegar revives the spirit and counts as a drink. The story shows how a public ruling against his view was misread.

people.name: Rav Giddel bar Menashe
people.about: The Sage who taught that the law does not follow Rabbi, then rebuked those who misread him.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, whose view that vinegar counts as a drink Rav Giddel rejected.

terms.meaning: Held guilty of breaking the fast, with the penalty that carries.
Latin for 'from the start': doing something in the first place, as opposed to accepting it after the fact.

11.note: A pregnant woman smelled food on Yom Kippur and craved it. People came to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who told them to whisper to her that it was Yom Kippur. They whispered to her, and it worked. Rabbi applied to her unborn child the verse 'Before I formed you in the belly I knew you', and the child born to her was Rabbi Yohanan.
11.why: The discussion turns to a pregnant woman who smells food on Yom Kippur. Right after, a second case is told in which the same whisper fails and the child grows up wicked, so the two stories are a pair.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who tells them to whisper to the woman that it is Yom Kippur.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The child born to that woman.

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, a full day's fast from food and drink.

12.note: Another pregnant woman smelled food on Yom Kippur and craved it. People came to Rabbi Hanina, who told them to whisper to her that it was Yom Kippur. They whispered, but she did not accept it and went on craving. Rabbi Hanina applied to her unborn child the verse 'The wicked are estranged from the womb', and the child born to her was Shabbetai, the hoarder of fruit, who held back fruit in famine years to raise its price.
12.why: It is paired with the story just before, where the same whisper worked and the child became Rabbi Yohanan. Next the Gemara turns to the mishna's rule on feeding a sick person on Yom Kippur.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: The Sage consulted about the pregnant woman's craving.

people.name: Shabbetai
people.about: The child born to her, known as the hoarder of fruits.

terms.meaning: Someone who bought up and held back food in famine years to drive up the price, at the cost of the poor.

13.note: Rav Nahman, citing Shmuel, says that a person seized with bulmos should be fed a sheep's tail with honey; Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua adds fine wheat flour with honey, and Rav Pappa even barley flour with honey. Rabbi Yohanan tells that once he was seized with bulmos and ran to the east side of a fig tree, where the figs ripen first, and so fulfilled the verse 'Wisdom preserves the lives of those who have it.' Rav Yosef taught that one who wants the taste of a fig should turn to its east side.
13.why: The Gemara has been discussing what to feed someone seized with bulmos, the dangerous hunger for which eating is allowed even on Yom Kippur. A baraita said honey and sweet foods restore his sight, and Abaye said sweets help only after other food.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Says, through Rav Nahman, to feed a sheep's tail with honey.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Reports Shmuel's remedy.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Adds fine wheat flour with honey.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Says even barley flour with honey helps.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Tells how he once ran to the east side of a fig tree when seized with bulmos.

terms.meaning: A sudden ravenous faintness that dims the eyes and can endanger life; the sufferer must be fed at once.

terms.term: east side of a fig tree
terms.meaning: The figs facing the sunrise ripen first, so that is where to find ripe fruit.

14.note: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei were walking on the road when Rabbi Yehuda was seized with bulmos. He overpowered a shepherd and ate his bread. Rabbi Yosei told him: you have robbed that shepherd. When they reached the city, Rabbi Yosei was seized with bulmos, and the townspeople surrounded him with jugs and plates. Rabbi Yehuda said to him: I robbed only the shepherd, but you have robbed the whole city.
14.why: The Gemara has been listing remedies for bulmos, the dangerous hunger that allows eating even on Yom Kippur. This story shows two Sages struck by it, and afterward the Gemara tells another story about the same travellers.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Seized with bulmos on the road, he takes a shepherd's bread.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: His companion, who scolds him and is then seized with bulmos himself in the city.

terms.meaning: A sudden ravenous faintness that can endanger life; the sufferer must be fed at once.

15.note: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei were travelling. Rabbi Meir read people's character from their names; the others did not. Their innkeeper's name was Kidor, which Rabbi Meir linked to the verse 'a generation of upheavals'. On Friday afternoon the other two left their purses with the innkeeper, but Rabbi Meir hid his at the grave of the innkeeper's father. The father appeared to the innkeeper in a dream and told him to take the purse there; told of the dream, the Sages said Friday-twilight dreams mean nothing, but Rabbi Meir guarded his money all day and then took it. The innkeeper denied ever getting the other purses. The Sages got him drunk, saw lentils on his mustache, and gave that sign to his wife, who handed the purses over. He went and killed his wife.
15.why: It follows the story of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei on the road. Afterward the Gemara ties it to a teaching that neglecting the washing after a meal can lead to killing: had the innkeeper washed his mouth, the lentils would not have shown.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage who reads character from names and does not trust the innkeeper.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A travelling companion who leaves his purse with the innkeeper.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The other companion, who also leaves his purse.

people.name: Kidor
people.about: The innkeeper, who denies receiving the purses and kills his wife.

terms.meaning: The time between sunset and dark on Friday, as Shabbat begins; the Sages say dreams then have no meaning.
A money pouch, left with the innkeeper for safekeeping over Shabbat, when money may not be carried.

16.note: Rabbi Yohanan suffered from tzefidna and went to a gentile matron known as a healer. She prepared medicine for him on Thursday and Friday. He asked what he should do on Shabbat; she said he would not need it. When he pressed her, she made him swear not to reveal the remedy. He swore 'to the God of Israel I will not reveal it', then went out and taught it in public. The Gemara explains that he meant he would not reveal it to God, but would to God's people, and that he told her so at the outset, so God's name was not desecrated.
16.why: The mishna has Rabbi Matya ben Harash allowing medicine to be put in the mouth of someone with throat pain on Shabbat. Afterward the Gemara says Rabbi Yohanan prepared this remedy on Shabbat, and Rav Hiyya bar Abba asks whether he relied on Rabbi Matya.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: A Sage suffering from tzefidna, who learns a remedy from a matron and makes it public.

people.name: matron
people.about: A gentile woman healer who treats Rabbi Yohanan and makes him swear to keep her remedy secret.

terms.meaning: An illness that starts in the teeth and gums, makes them bleed, and then spreads to the intestines.
A noble gentile woman, here a well-known healer.
An act that makes God or God's people look bad in the eyes of others, such as a great Sage seeming to break an oath.

17.note: Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya were walking on the road, with Levi HaSadar and Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya behind them, when they were asked how we know that saving a life overrides Shabbat. Rabbi Yishmael argued from the burglar who may be killed even though it is unclear he came to kill. Rabbi Akiva argued from the murderer-priest who is taken even off the altar if he can testify to save a life: if the Temple service, which overrides Shabbat, gives way to a doubtful chance of saving a life, all the more so does Shabbat. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya argued: if circumcision, which concerns one limb, overrides Shabbat, all the more so does saving the whole body.
17.why: The Gemara has been ruling on clearing rubble from a person trapped on Shabbat. It now seeks the source for setting Shabbat aside to save a life; more proofs follow, and Rava says only Shmuel's proof, 'and live by them', cannot be refuted.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: Argues from the case of the burglar breaking in.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Argues from the priest taken from the altar to save a life.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Argues from circumcision, which overrides Shabbat.

people.name: Levi HaSadar
people.about: A younger Sage walking behind the three.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Also walking behind the elder Sages.

terms.meaning: An argument from a lesser case to a greater: if something holds in a light case, it holds all the more in a weighty one.
The Sabbath, the weekly day of rest on which work is forbidden.
God's presence dwelling among the people of Israel.

18.note: Rabbi Yirmeya had offended Rabbi Abba, and went and sat at the threshold of Rabbi Abba's house to beg forgiveness. Rabbi Abba's maid poured out dirty water and it landed on Rabbi Yirmeya's head. He said, 'They have made me into a trash heap', and applied to himself the verse 'Who lifts up the needy out of the trash heap.' Rabbi Abba heard, came out to him, and said: now I must go out to appease you, as it is written, 'Go, humble yourself and urge your neighbor.'
18.why: Rabbi Yitzhak has just taught that one who angers a friend, even by words, must appease him, from the same verse Rabbi Abba quotes. The story shows the obligation turning around once the apologizer is himself insulted.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Offended Rabbi Abba and sat at his door to seek forgiveness.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: The offended Sage, who ends up seeking to appease Rabbi Yirmeya.

terms.meaning: To ask forgiveness of someone you have wronged until they are reconciled.

19.note: A butcher had insulted Rav and did not come to apologize. On the eve of Yom Kippur Rav said he would go and make peace with him. On the way he met Rav Huna, who asked where he was going; when Rav told him, Rav Huna said, 'Abba is going to kill a person.' Rav went and stood before the butcher, who was splitting an animal's head. The butcher looked up and said, 'Are you Abba? Go, I have nothing to say to you.' As he split the head, a bone flew out, struck him in the throat, and killed him.
19.why: The Gemara has been teaching how one must seek forgiveness, especially before Yom Kippur, and has just told how Rabbi Zeira made himself available to anyone who had wronged him. Here Rav goes further and seeks out the man who wronged him.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage, called Abba here, who goes to make peace with the butcher who insulted him.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Rav's student, who predicts that the visit will cost the butcher his life.

people.name: butcher
people.about: An unnamed man who insulted Rav and refuses to make peace.

terms.meaning: The day before the Day of Atonement, when people seek forgiveness from those they have wronged.

20.note: Rav was reading a Torah portion aloud before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. When Rabbi Hiyya came in, Rav went back to the beginning; when bar Kappara came in, and then Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi, he went back again each time. When Rabbi Hanina bar Hama came in, Rav said, 'Shall I go back so many times?' and did not. Rabbi Hanina was offended. Rav went to him on the eve of Yom Kippur for thirteen years to appease him, but he would not be appeased.
20.why: Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina has taught that one need not ask forgiveness more than three times, so the Gemara asks how Rav could ask thirteen times and how Rabbi Hanina could refuse. It explains Rabbi Hanina's refusal with a dream about Rav's future.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Reads the Torah portion and later seeks Rabbi Hanina's forgiveness for thirteen years.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, before whom Rav was reading.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Rav's uncle and teacher, for whom Rav starts over.

people.name: bar Kappara
people.about: A Sage for whom Rav starts over.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Ḥama
people.about: The Sage for whom Rav does not start over, and who is offended.

terms.meaning: A section of the Torah read aloud; here Rav was reciting it before his teacher.
